KEY MESSAGE 1...Very comfortable temperatures this weekend with 
mainly dry conditions.

Clear skies and light winds early this morning are supporting 
effective radiational cooling. Lows fall into the 50s across the 
cooler outlying locations, while urban centers remain near 60 
degrees by sunrise. Given these conditions, areas of valley fog have 
begun to develop and can be seen on satellite imagery using the 
Nighttime Microphysics RGB, with fog gradually filling the valleys. 
Any morning fog will erode with daytime heating and lift by mid-
morning.

Quiet weather is the theme for the weekend as high pressure 
originating from northern Canada settles across the Northeast 
through the first half of Sunday. However, there remains a very low 
chance for an isolated shower from mid to late afternoon, mainly 
across eastern Massachusetts, as a potent mid-level shortwave with 
an associated cold pool of -18C brushes the eastern fringes of the 
region. Given PWATs are quite low, between 0.6 and 0.8 inches, and a 
notably dry airmass remains in place, the threat for a stray shower 
is very low. Our thinking is that this robust shortwave will result 
in more cloud cover than anything else across eastern areas.

Temperatures remain seasonable, with highs generally ranging from 
the upper 70s to lower 80s. Another cool night is expected Saturday 
night, with clear skies and light winds supporting effective 
radiational cooling. Lows fall into the lower to middle 50s across 
the cooler outlying locations, while urban centers remain near 60 
degrees.

Despite the pleasant weather, a moderate risk for rip currents is 
expected today and Sunday. Those heading to the beach should 
remain aware of local conditions and check with lifeguards or 
beach staff regarding rip current risks at their specific 
location.

High pressure begins to shift offshore Sunday as a low pressure 
system approaches from the Great Lakes. Increasing warm air 
advection will bring increasing clouds through the afternoon, while 
temperatures remain seasonable in the upper 70s and lower 80s. 
Humidity will gradually increase as dew points rise into the lower 
60s. Most, if not all, of the daylight hours remain dry, with the 
next opportunity for rainfall arriving Sunday night into Monday.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Rain returns late Sunday into Monday, followed by 
quieter weather through most of next week.

Confidence remains high that most, if not all, of the daylight hours 
Sunday remain dry. Rainfall arrives late Sunday, with the steadiest 
rain anticipated overnight through early Monday. We are now entering 
the time range where high-resolution guidance can begin to better 
resolve this period. While some guidance brings rain into western 
Massachusetts and western Connecticut as early as late afternoon, 
prior to sunset, ensemble guidance supports a later arrival, with 
measurable rainfall generally arriving between 8 PM and midnight.

There is increasing certainty in the overall evolution of this 
system, with one area of low pressure likely passing across northern 
New England and a secondary low tracking south of New England across 
the Mid-Atlantic. This evolution is also supported by the ECMWF EFI 
and Shift of Tails for QPF, which highlight both of these regions. 
With southern New England positioned between these two areas, 
confidence in the highest rainfall totals occurring across the 
region has diminished, lowering the threat for widespread flash 
flooding.

However, PWATs increase to between 1.8 and 2.1 inches overnight into 
Monday, supporting the potential for locally heavier downpours. A 
Marginal Risk for Excessive Rainfall (level 1 of 4) remains in place 
for much of New England Sunday night into Monday, primarily due to 
the potential for localized flash flooding. Ensemble guidance 
currently supports a general range of 0.25 to 0.50 inches across 
southern New England, though localized higher amounts are possible, 
especially beneath heavier downpours.

Given the expected cloud cover and showers, Monday will be cooler, 
with highs generally ranging from the mid-70s to around 80 degrees. 
It will also be fairly humid, with dew points remaining elevated and 
resulting in rather sticky conditions.

KEY MESSAGE 3...Seasonably warm temperatures and moderate humidity 
return through the middle of next week, followed by increasing 
shower chances late in the week.

Drier air advects in from the northwest beginning Monday night into 
Tuesday, leading to another dry stretch Tuesday through Wednesday, 
and possibly into the first half of Thursday, as surface high 
pressure builds back into the region. Temperatures remain 
seasonable, with highs in the lower to middle 80s and tolerable 
humidity as dew points remain in the lower to middle 60s. Ensemble 
guidance continues to signal a transition toward more unsettled 
weather late in the week, with shower chances returning and 
temperatures potentially trending slightly below normal.
